# R2 Digest — Provan, *1 and 2 Kings* (NIBC), §13–§18

**Source:** Iain W. Provan, *1 and 2 Kings*, NIBC (1995)
**Slice:** `R2_solomon_prayer_apostasy_1221-1528.txt` (raw lines 1221–1528)
**Scope:** §13 Solomon’s Prayer (1 Kgs. 8:22–53); §14 Temple Narrative Ended (8:54–9:9); §15 Glory under a Cloud (9:10–10:29); §16 Apostasy (11:1–13); §17 Opposition and Death (11:14–43); **§18 Excursus: Solomon in Canonical Context**
**Extractor note:** Claims only; no live wiki edits. Attribution is to Provan throughout.

---

### C-R2-01 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Provan treats Solomon’s prayer (1 Kgs. 8:22–53) as of great importance for understanding Kings as a whole: after temple–Davidic-promise linkage (vv. 22–26), reflections on God’s “dwelling” (vv. 27–30), a seven-fold petition (vv. 31–51), and a summarizing tailpiece (vv. 52–53).
**Quote:** “Solomon now turns to address God in a prayer that is of great importance for our understanding of the book of Kings as a whole.”
**Locus:** §13 intro; slice lines 11–12; 1 Kgs. 8:22–53
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R2-02 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** The first part of the prayer (8:22–26) picks up the third part of the divine promise to David: an eternal dynasty; Solomon asks God to fulfill “You shall never fail to have a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel.”
**Quote:** “The main concern of the first part of the prayer is to pick up the third part of the divine promise to David that has already been alluded to in verses 15–21: the promise of an eternal dynasty.”
**Locus:** §13 on 8:22–26; slice lines 13–14
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[solomon]], [[david]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

---

### C-R2-03 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Provan notes the conditional form of the dynasty promise (as in 1 Kgs. 2:4) does not match 2 Sam. 7:11–16; by 8:25 the reader has hints that Solomon sits by grace, not wholehearted obedience, heightening tension between conditional and unconditional aspects.
**Quote:** “We last came across this promise, with its conditional form, in 1 Kings 2:4, and we noted there the curious way in which its terms do not, in fact, match up with the terms as described in 2 Samuel 7:11–16. … The repetition in 8:25, then, of the Davidic promise as phrased in 1 Kings 2:4, serves only to heighten the tension between its conditional and unconditional aspects that we first noted in 2:4.”
**Locus:** §13 on 8:22–26; slice lines 13–14
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[solomon]], [[david]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

---

### C-R2-04 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** For Provan, God’s choices ultimately outweigh frail human choices: the Davidic promise can delay judgment (e.g. 2 Kgs. 8:19), and the prayer itself (vv. 31–51) opens forgiveness after judgment; God’s graciousness is “as incomparable as any of God’s other attributes.”
**Quote:** “Yet God’s graciousness is as incomparable as any of God’s other attributes. Thus, we shall hear in passages such as 2 Kings 8:19 of the Davidic promise delaying God’s judgment and in this prayer (vv. 31–51) of the possibility of forgiveness after judgment. God’s choices are always in the end more important than the choices made by mere mortals, in all their frailty and sinfulness.”
**Locus:** §13 on 8:22–26; slice lines 13–14
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]]

### C-R2-05 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Temple is not where God *is* but where God’s Name is; God hears from heaven; even the highest heaven cannot contain God; prayer *toward* the temple (not physical presence in it) suffices.
**Quote:** “God cannot dwell on earth (v. 27). The temple—in spite of the statement of verse 13—is not to be thought of as a place where God is but only as a place where God’s Name is, a place towards which God’s eyes are open (v. 29; cf. Isa. 66:1–3). The hearing of prayer is done from heaven (v. 30). … Being utterly transcendent, God cannot be ‘placed’ at all… it is sufficient for people to pray toward the temple rather than be physically in it (vv. 29–30; cf. John 4:21–24).”
**Locus:** §13 on 8:27–30; slice lines 15–16
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R2-06 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Seven petitions: (1) legal/priestly judgment when evidence fails (vv. 31–32); (2–4) defeat/exile, drought, famine/plague/siege as sin-caused disasters needing forgiveness (and instruction, v. 36); (5) foreigner who prays toward the temple (vv. 41–43); (6) victory when army fights as executive of God’s justice (vv. 44–45); (7) major concern—defeat, exile, repentance, prayer toward land/city/temple, restoration as inheritance/people of the Exodus (vv. 46–51).
**Quote:** “Its length, and the fact that it returns to a topic already dealt with, identifies this [seventh petition] as the major concern of the prayer. … Surely a second Exodus, from a different land, is not beyond the bounds of possibility!”
**Locus:** §13 on 8:31–51; slice lines 17–20
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

---

### C-R2-07 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** The seven petitions differ sharply in atmosphere from 8:23–26: there, necessity of obedience; here, human disobedience is presupposed (“there is no one who does not sin,” v. 46), and the prayer moves to divine forgiveness and grace—hinting that God’s choices, not Israel’s, are crucial.
**Quote:** “What is striking about these seven petitions is how different they are in atmosphere from the first part of the prayer in verses 23–26. There the stress was upon the necessity of obedience. Here, however, human disobedience is simply presupposed (esp. in v. 46: there is no one who does not sin), and the prayer moves beyond God’s judgment to dependence upon divine forgiveness and grace.”
**Locus:** §13 on 8:31–51; slice lines 22–23
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[davidic-covenant]]

### C-R2-08 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Land-as-inheritance and people-brought-out-of-Egypt language grounds restoration hope in Abrahamic promise (Gen. 12; 17) and Exodus election, not law-keeping ability; foreign worshiper (vv. 41–43) also recalls Abrahamic horizon.
**Quote:** “The land is the land given to the fathers (i.e., the patriarchs, vv. 34, 40), the land given as an inheritance (v. 36; cf. Deut. 4:37–38)—statements that remind us, like the case of the foreign worshiper in verses 41–43, of the divine promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:1–3; 17:1–8. The people … brought out of Egypt are Abraham’s descendants, delivered from oppression not because of their ability to keep the law but simply because of the promise.”
**Locus:** §13 on 8:31–51; slice lines 22–23
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R2-09 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Closing of the prayer (8:52–53) returns to gracious election; for Provan, “grace always underpins law and provides it with its broader context.”
**Quote:** “It is to this question of gracious election that Solomon returns as he brings his prayer to a close… The repetition simply underlines the reality of the way in which grace always underpins law and provides it with its broader context.”
**Locus:** §13 on 8:52–53; slice lines 24–25
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[davidic-covenant]]

### C-R2-10 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Theological thesis of the prayer: temple and law placed in wider perspective—God is not confined by/dependent on the temple and will hear prayers in exile after its destruction; obedience still judges kings, yet Solomon holds out hope that grace will have the last word.
**Quote:** “Solomon’s prayer is of the utmost importance, for it places both the temple and the law in wider perspective. … God, who is not confined by a building and who is certainly not dependent upon it, will survive even its destruction and hear the people’s prayers in exile. … Yet Solomon holds out hope for restoration beyond failure, for he holds out hope that grace will have the last word.”
**Locus:** §13 summary; slice lines 26–27
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R2-11 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Additional note: woes in the seven petitions track Deut. 28 covenant curses; 8:46–53 consciously uses Deut. 29:17–27 for exile-reversal; Provan holds 8:34 is explicit about restoration to the land, modifying McConville’s claim that Kings and Deut. 30:1–10 differ on Israel’s future if 8:33–34 and 46–53 are read as one text.
**Quote:** “It seems certain that the woes in Solomon’s seven petitions have been chosen because they appear in the list of covenant curses for disobedience in Deut. 28:15–68… First Kings 8:34 is quite explicit about Israel’s restoration to the land.”
**Locus:** Additional Notes §13 on 8:33; slice lines 49–50

### C-R2-12 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Solomon’s second address (8:54–61) celebrates Moses promises (including “rest” = establishment in Canaan) and desires Israel to walk in God’s ways so that “all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God”; Provan reads a universalistic “kingdom of priests” vocation (Gen. 12; Exod. 19:6; Isa. 49:6).
**Quote:** “Here again we see a rather universalistic idea of Israel’s role in the world (cf. vv. 41–43). Israel is to be ‘a kingdom of priests,’ mediating God to the Gentiles and bringing God’s salvation to the ends of the earth (cf. Gen. 12:1–3; Exod. 19:6; Isa. 49:6).”
**Locus:** §14 on 8:54–61; slice lines 72–73
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R2-13 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Dedication festivities (8:62–66) picture a happy, unified kingdom from Egypt to Euphrates (cf. ch. 4); Provan foreshadows the ironic “to their tents” of 12:16—days of joy strictly numbered.
**Quote:** “This picture of a happy, unified kingdom stretching from Egypt to the Euphrates very much corresponds to the picture in chapter 4. It will not be so very long now, however, before Israelites will be found going ‘to their tents’ for a very different reason and in a very different mood (12:16).”
**Locus:** §14 on 8:62–66; slice lines 74–75

### C-R2-14 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Second divine appearance (9:1–9) marks the endpoint of Solomon’s upward mobility and points ahead to disaster: temple as prayer-focus assured (v. 3), dynasty request answered (vv. 4–5), but future of temple, dynasty, and land depends on obedience of Solomon and later generations—especially against idolatry.
**Quote:** “This second appearance of God marks the endpoint of Solomon’s upward mobility and points us ahead to disaster. … The future of the temple and the dynasty, however—as well as possession of the very land itself (v. 7)—is made dependent upon obedience: the obedience of Solomon (9:4) and the obedience of future generations of Israelites…”
**Locus:** §14 on 9:1–9; slice lines 76–77

### C-R2-15 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Read with 8:22–53, the “if” of 9:6 is effectively a “when” (8:46): obedience will give way to apostasy; the temple is no sooner built than its inevitable end is announced; empire no sooner created than its destruction is heard of.
**Quote:** “To read 9:1–9 in the light of 8:22–53 is to see immediately, then, the inevitability of disaster. The if of verse 6 cannot in reality be anything other than a when (8:46). Obedience will inevitably give way to apostasy. … The temple is no sooner built than we hear of its inevitable end; the empire is no sooner created than we hear of its inevitable destruction.”
**Locus:** §14 on 9:1–9; slice lines 76–77
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R2-16 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** 9:10–10:29 re-presents Solomonic glory “under a cloud,” destined to fade; not mere repetition of chs. 4–5 but rewritten so themes hint foolishness (Hiram dealings, forced labor, foreigners listening to wisdom) and remind of earlier folly; “last chapter” of the golden age.
**Quote:** “It is therefore glory under a cloud, destined to fade away. … Themes from chapters 4–5 are picked up now in a way that hints, not of wisdom, but of foolishness… we are forced to be aware, even as we hear of accumulating gold and proverbial splendor (cf. Matt. 6:29), that we are reading the last chapter of the story of Solomon’s ‘golden age’—that he is heading very shortly for a fall.”
**Locus:** §15 intro; slice lines 98–101
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R2-17 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Gold floods 9:10–10:29 (120 → 420 → 666 talents; exotic sources); Provan resists reading it only as fulfillment of promised riches (3:13): delayed appearance after 9:6–9 warning, contrast with food-prosperity shared with subjects in chs. 4–5, and texts like Prov. 30:8 and Deut. 17:17 make excessive wealth a danger of apostasy; court luxury vs shared prosperity.
**Quote:** “Excessive wealth brings with it the danger of apostasy. … What is particularly striking about 1 Kings 9:10–10:29 when compared with 1 Kings 4–5 is the manner in which the authors go out of their way in 4–5 to emphasize that the prosperity of the king was shared with his subjects… This is a theme that is notable for its absence in 9:10–10:29, where all the emphasis lies upon the luxury of the royal court…”
**Locus:** §15 on 9:10–14; slice lines 102–107
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R2-18 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Forced labor section delayed until now associates Canaanite laborers (whom Deut. 7 required to be ḥrm) with Pharaoh’s daughter (3:1; Deut. 7 intermarriage warnings); living Canaanites + Egyptian marriage prepare Solomon’s seduction by other gods (11:4); temporary temple orthodoxy (9:25) is cold comfort.
**Quote:** “Their appearance (very much alive) along with Pharaoh’s daughter in 1 Kings 9 again serves to prepare us for Solomon’s downfall. Like later kings (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:7–8), he will indeed be seduced by the other gods (11:4).”

### C-R2-19 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Queen of Sheba episode reframes “worldwide fame” from ch. 4: her praise narrows blessing to court officials’ enjoyment of wise words; ch. 10 focuses benefits of wisdom on court/Solomon, luxury influx, self-indulgence—recalling 1 Sam. 8 warnings; Provan asks whether “wise words” have displaced wise action for the people.

**Claim (notes):** Cabul more likely from ḵḇl “fetters” (Ps. 149:8) than “waste away”—fitting Hiram as junior/fettered partner; Pharaoh’s capture of Gezer shows Solomon *could* have ḥrm’d Canaanites but chose to keep them for building enthusiasm; Queen of Sheba visit cited in Matt. 12:42 / Luke 11:31 (“one greater than Solomon”).

### C-R2-22 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Throughout 1 Kgs. 1–10 authors only *hinted* heart trouble; prayer + 9:1–9 made law and consequences clear; 9:10–10:29 is climbing before the fall; ch. 11 opens open critique—return to marriage/worship theme of 3:1–3; sins found him out → apostasy.
**Quote:** “That fall is now reported as the authors, returning to the marriage/worship theme of 3:1–3, come out in open critique of Solomon and describe the inevitable consequences of all that has gone before. His sins have found him out, and they have led him to apostasy.”

### C-R2-23 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Solomon “loved the LORD” (3:3) yet also loved Pharaoh’s daughter and many foreign women, “held fast” (dḇq) to them—verbs of Deut. wholehearted loyalty to God; heart divided (11:4); wives turn him after other gods; “did evil in the eyes of the LORD”; ceases to be like David (who never worshiped other gods); builds rival sanctuaries on Mount of Olives etc. for “all” foreign gods.
**Quote:** “The Israelite was to love the LORD wholeheartedly (Deut. 6:5). But Solomon’s heart was divided (v. 4); he was a man unable to practice his own advice to his subjects (8:61). … hints of impropriety become direct accusation: Solomon did evil in the eyes of the LORD (v. 6). … Solomon not only worships them, he builds sanctuaries for them on the Mount of Olives… and elsewhere that rival the temple… His ‘turning away’ is truly spectacular.”
**Locus:** §16 on 11:1–8; slice lines 174–175
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[david]], [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R2-24 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** God angry; kingdom to be torn away (11:11)—expected from 2:4, 8:25, 9:4–5—yet recall of Samuel to Saul (1 Sam. 15:28) correlates Saul with Solomon, deepening 2 Sam. 7 tension (conditional continuity vs non-Saul-like punishment of successors).
**Quote:** “First Kings 11:11 only adds to this second reader’s sense of puzzlement, because it so obviously recalls Samuel’s words to Saul in 1 Samuel 15:28, thus correlating Saul with Solomon.”
**Locus:** §16 on 11:9–13; slice lines 176–177

### C-R2-25 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Deferred / mitigated judgment: not during Solomon’s lifetime (11:12); not whole kingdom but eleven tribes—one tribe remains “out of grace, for the sake of David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen” (11:13). Readers of Kings (law) get more than expected; readers of 2 Sam. 7 (grace) get less—middle ground between rigid law and boundless grace; this stance continues much of Kings (Judah retained “for the sake of David,” e.g. 1 Kgs. 15:4; 2 Kgs. 8:19); law will *appear* to prevail in 2 Kgs. 24–25.
**Quote:** “Everyone ends up surprised, standing unexpectedly on middle ground somewhere between rigid law and boundless grace. This is, indeed, where we shall be standing for much of the remainder of the book: one tribe (Judah) will remain due to God’s grace, ‘for the sake of David,’ for a very long time… Eventually, law will appear to prevail (2 Kgs. 24–25)…”
**Locus:** §16 on 11:9–13; slice lines 176–177
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R2-28 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Two adversaries raised by God: Hadad of Edom (exodus-like sojourn in Egypt; liberated by Pharaoh who does *not* harden his heart—ironically set on Solomon by Egypt, once treated as friend via 3:1 marriage); Rezon of Damascus/Aram from the north. Peace of 5:4 fractured.
**Quote:** “Solomon’s first adversary is thus, ironically, set upon him by an old enemy of Israel whom he had unwisely treated as a friend (1 Kgs. 3:1). … Rezon opposes the king from the north, Hadad from the south. Where there was peace on all sides, now there are only enemies.”
**Locus:** §17 on 11:14–25; slice lines 225–229
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R2-29 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Ahijah tears new cloak (śalmâ ≈ consonants of Solomon) into twelve pieces; ten to Jeroboam; one tribe for David/Jerusalem—math odd (10+1≠12) because Benjamin (with Judah) is presupposed (12:21); “they have forsaken me” (plural): king models/represents people’s apostasy.
**Quote:** “Solomon’s abandonment of God, it should be noted, is also the people’s abandonment of God. This is demonstrated in the plural phrase, they have forsaken me, which reflects the way that in the book of Kings, kings are characteristically models for and representative of the behavior of their subjects.”
**Locus:** §17 on 11:26–33; Additional Notes 11:30–32; slice lines 230–231, 265–267

### C-R2-30 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim:** Mitigation repeated (11:34–39): no tribal loss in Solomon’s lifetime; son keeps one tribe so David always has a “lamp… in Jerusalem”; Jeroboam promised David-like dynasty *if* obedient—but promise already conceals expected failure; division “not forever” (v. 39)—reunion hoped; punishment is fatherly discipline (2 Sam. 7:14) not eternal Saul-like rejection (despite surface parallel); grace not only mitigates judgment but transforms it into blessing; hope against 2 Kgs. 24–25.
**Quote:** “Though it appears that God has treated Solomon very much like Saul (in spite of 2 Sam. 7:15), in reality he is merely handing down fatherly discipline (2 Sam. 7:14). … Law does indeed appear to prevail in the last Judean king’s loss of his throne at the end of Kings. But law is not in the end more powerful than grace, and grace, 11:39 implies, does not function only to mitigate judgment, but ultimately to transform it into blessing.”
**Locus:** §17 on 11:34–39; slice lines 232–233
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[solomon]], [[david]], [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R2-33 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Excursus summary of Solomon):** Mostly wise, but wisdom not always honorable (2:13–46) and later degenerates into self-indulgent word-games (10:1–13); mostly committed to God, yet early integrity question marks and wayward heart → accumulated indiscretions become outright apostasy (11:1–8); ideal king/kingdom always in tension with reality; most of all blessed by God.
**Quote:** “He was for the most part a wise king, although his wisdom was not always used for honorable ends (1 Kgs. 2:13–46), and towards the end of his reign it had degenerated into a self-indulgent playing of games with words (1 Kgs. 10:1–13). … Eventually his accumulated individual indiscretions turned to outright apostasy… He was, most of all, a king blessed by God.”
**Locus:** §18 Excursus; slice lines 288–289
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R2-34 — Claim / Quote / Locus / Targets
**Claim (Excursus — law/grace synthesis):** Solomon believed eternal dynasty blessing tied to moral virtue (father’s and his—2:2–4; 9:3–9); blessing continued through indiscretion; 1 Kgs. 11 shows more to God’s dealings with David’s house than David told (2 Sam. 7 horizon); punishment less bad initially (11:12–13, 32, 34, 36) and not eternal (11:39); God’s choice more important than human choices, without permitting presumption that evades law.
**Quote:** “Eventually it appeared that God’s choice was in the end indeed to be more important than human choices, even if mortals could never presume on grace in order to evade the demands of law.”
**Locus:** §18 Excursus; slice lines 288–289

## Key theses (for integrator)

### On the prayer (§13) as theological heart
1. **Name-theology / transcendence:** Temple is place of the Name and orientation for prayer, not divine containment; God hears from heaven and survives temple destruction.
2. **Obedience vs grace dual register:** 8:23–26 presses conditional dynasty obedience; 8:31–51 presupposes universal sin and petitions forgiveness—grace underpins law.
3. **Major petition = exile/restoration:** Second-Exodus hope for the inheritance people; foreigner’s access keeps Abrahamic horizon open.
4. **Canonical function in Kings:** Grounds later hope that grace, not only curse, frames the story after 2 Kgs. 24–25.

### On conditional / unconditional Davidic promise
- Tension sustained from 2:4 vs 2 Sam. 7 through 8:25, 9:4–9, 11:11–13, 11:34–39.
- **Deferred judgment:** not in Solomon’s lifetime; one tribe (Judah + presupposed Benjamin) retained for David and Jerusalem.
- **Fatherly discipline** not Saul-like eternal rejection (11:39); grace mitigates *and* ultimately transforms judgment; lamp in Jerusalem.

### On wisdom → apostasy arc
- Glory of 9–10 rewritten under cloud of 8–9: gold, court luxury, Deut. 17 abrogations, Canaanite labor + foreign marriage → ch. 11 open apostasy (divided heart, high places, evil in LORD’s eyes).

### On §18 Solomon in Canonical Context (must preserve densely)
- **OT close:** blessing > human virtue; hope at exile’s end if David’s son always reigns (forgive / restore throne / reconstitute people).
- **NT type:** Jesus = Son of David / greater than Solomon / Wisdom of God; perfect integration of wisdom + obedience; typological echoes (e.g. entry/coronation).
- **NT warning:** Solomon’s splendor as anti-anxiety / anti-hoarding foil; “one of us.”
- **Wisdom for disciples:** from-above wisdom to “children” // 1 Kgs. 3:7; dangers of below-wisdom.
- **Temple:** superseded (Stephen; church as temple / Christ’s body) yet still necessary intertext for Hebrews/Revelation heavenly temple.
